title: Pressure-cooker congee
subtitle: Silky rice porridge in 20 minutes
excerpt: Long-grain rice cooked under pressure with stock into a thick, smooth rice porridge. A deeply comforting dish across East and Southeast Asia, plain and restorative, or dressed with toppings.
sourceNotes: Congee (jook in Cantonese, zhou in Mandarin, kayu in Japanese) is eaten across East and Southeast Asia. It is a staple restorative dish, served plain or with accompaniments. The pressure-cooker method compresses the traditional 1 to 2 hour stovetop simmer to about 20 minutes and produces an excellent silky result.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Congee thickens significantly on standing. Reheat with extra stock or water.

content.text: Congee is rice cooked in a large volume of liquid until the grains completely break down into a smooth, silky porridge. It has a neutral, slightly savoury flavour on its own, a canvas for toppings rather than a finished dish. The pressure cooker produces a fully broken-down congee in 20 minutes where the stovetop requires nearly two hours of stirring.

Use a 1:10 ratio of rice to liquid. This sounds like a lot of liquid but is necessary, the rice absorbs and releases starch throughout the long cook, and congee that finishes too thick will set solid on cooling.

Serve plain with a drizzle of sesame oil, or topped with sliced spring onion, a soft-boiled egg, crispy shallots, ginger, white pepper, and soy sauce. The plain porridge is the comfort; the toppings are the meal.

Put the rinsed rice, {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock, ginger, garlic, and soy sauce in the pressure cooker. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of at least 10 minutes.

Open the lid and stir, the congee may look liquid on top and thick below. Stir vigorously to combine. Remove the ginger and garlic. Taste and adjust seasoning. Ladle into bowls and add toppings at the table.

rows.cause: The rice absorbed all the liquid during the natural release.
rows.fix: Stir in additional hot stock or water until you reach a pourable, porridge-like consistency.

rows.symptom: The rice grains are still visible and distinct
rows.cause: The pressure was insufficient or the rice was not fully cooked.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 10 minutes. Congee requires the grains to break down completely.

content.text: Congee is restorative food, eaten when unwell, after a long night, or when warmth and ease are more important than flavour. It is the rice equivalent of chicken soup in terms of what it does for the person eating it. The toppings can be elaborate or entirely absent. The pressure cooker makes the two-hour simmer into a 20-minute task.
